# About this book {.unnumbered #sec-about}

LightHit computes the light that the optical modules of a neutrino telescope
see, without following individual photons. A photon emitted in water reaches a
module directly, arrives after one or more scattering events, or is absorbed.
Instead of sampling that random walk, the package solves the radiative transfer
equation for the photon distribution and evaluates the part of it that a given
module registers.

This book follows one route from end to end: the spectral transfer equation, a
Fourier-adjoint Green's function, a real Cherenkov source, a module that looks
in a definite direction, and the expected number of photoelectrons in each time
bin. Every step is given three times over --- as the physics, as the discrete
algorithm, and as the symbols in `src/lighthit` that implement it --- so that a
reader can check a formula against the code without reading the code first.

## What the book covers {.unnumbered #sec-about-scope}

@sec-overview states the problem the package solves and lays out the whole
computation on one page; the remaining chapters expand one box of that map
each. Part I fixes the physics and the observable: the spectral transfer
equation (@sec-spectral-rte) and the optical module (@sec-optical-module). Part
II builds the Green's function in an infinite homogeneous medium --- the
Fourier-adjoint formulation (@sec-fourier-adjoint), the angular system with its
exact free tail (@sec-angular-system), the separation of scattering orders and
the spatial inversion (@sec-scattering-orders), and the passage back to time
(@sec-time-and-bins). Part III replaces the point flash by a real source and the
point receiver by a real module: the spectral Cherenkov emission
(@sec-cherenkov-source), tracks and showers (@sec-track-and-shower), and the
exact directional module (@sec-directional-om). Part IV is the production
scheme itself: the cache and its cost (@sec-cache-and-memory), the end-to-end
algorithm (@sec-rte-to-pe), the weak-module threshold
(@sec-weak-module-threshold), the public interface (@sec-api-and-viewer), and
the error budget (@sec-validation).

The appendices carry what would interrupt that route: notation (@sec-notation),
the special-function identities the derivations use (@sec-identities), the
independent reference solutions that the main text compares against
(@sec-reference-solutions), the methods that were tried and rejected
(@sec-rejected-methods), the benchmark protocol (@sec-benchmark-protocol), and
a catalogue of scripts, tests and file formats (@sec-catalogue).

## How a chapter is built {.unnumbered #sec-about-structure}

Every chapter in the main route has the same nine sections, in the same order:
the physical question; the assumptions and definitions it rests on; the
derivation; the discrete algorithm; the correspondence with the code; a worked
number; the checks that number passed; the range of validity; and exercises
with the notebook that goes with them.

The reason for the fixed shape is that the three failure modes of a book like
this one are different and are caught in different places. A wrong formula is
caught in the derivation. A formula that is right but implemented differently
is caught by the correspondence table, which names the function that evaluates
each expression. A formula that is right and implemented faithfully but used
outside its range is caught by the range-of-validity section, which states what
breaks first and at which parameter.

## What "solution" means here {.unnumbered #sec-about-solution}

The book distinguishes an exact solution of the original transfer equation, an
exact solution of an approximated equation, and a numerical estimate of one
observable. Truncating the scattering operator at angular degree $L$
approximates the transfer equation; the linear system built from that
truncation is then solved exactly, including an exact treatment of the infinite
free tail above $L$. "All orders of scattering" is scoped the same way:
increasing the number of retained angular moments and increasing the number of
scattering events summed are different knobs, and both are reported separately
wherever they matter.

Exactness claims in this book are therefore always qualified by the
approximation they are exact *within*. Where a step is exact in the stronger
sense --- the ballistic term, the angular integrals of the Cherenkov cone, and
the physical-time binning used by the ballistic contribution --- it is said so
explicitly. The production event route currently Fourier-inverts both scattered
components; that distinction is stated wherever time bins are discussed.

## How numbers are reported {.unnumbered #sec-about-numbers}

A numerical result in this book is quoted together with the configuration that
produced it, the name of the algorithm or benchmark set, the number of threads,
whether a warm-up run preceded it, the number of repetitions, the median and
the spread, and the script that reproduces it. Timings without that envelope
are not comparable between machines and are not quoted.

Figures and tables name the script that regenerates them. Where a number
depends on private optical data that is not distributed with the package, the
text says so and gives the public synthetic configuration that produces a
number of the same shape.

## How the code is referenced {.unnumbered #sec-about-code}

Code is referenced by stable symbols --- `lighthit.angular.resolvent_rows`,
`lighthit.directional.DirectionalCache`,
`lighthit.transport.TransportKernel.transport` --- never by line number. A
correspondence table in each chapter maps every displayed formula to the symbol
that evaluates it. If a symbol in this book does not exist in the package, that
is a defect in the book and not a naming convention.

Modules under `lighthit.experimental` are research code: they are reachable
from the public interface only with an explicit opt-in, and the book marks them
as such wherever they appear.

## What the book does not cover {.unnumbered #sec-about-excluded}

The medium is homogeneous and unbounded. Polarisation, the water--air and
water--ice boundaries, shadowing by the detector structure, and inelastic
scattering are outside the model. Detector electronics, trigger and noise are
outside the package: the observable computed here is the expected number of
photoelectrons per module and per time bin, which is the input to a readout
simulation rather than its output.

The development history is also outside the main route. Methods that were
tried and abandoned are described in @sec-rejected-methods, as reproducible
experiments with a stated hypothesis, an acceptance criterion, the measurement
that failed it, and whatever remained useful --- not as a narrative of who
proposed what and when.

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered #sec-about-prerequisites}

Derivatives, multivariate integrals, linear algebra and elementary probability
are assumed. Spherical-harmonic and operator notation is introduced where it is
first needed, and collected in @sec-notation. The reference implementation is
in `src/lighthit`; the executable notebooks under `notebooks/course` illustrate
the methods chapter by chapter. A notebook is an illustration: it is never the
only place a number in this book comes from, and never the only proof of a
statement.
